The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 41 would write two rules into the California Constitution. First, programs funded by new state special taxes would face independent audits by the state auditor. These audits would occur when the ballot initiative is initially proposed and then every four years after a special tax takes effect. Second, no new state tax could circumvent the Gann limit, the voter-approved spending cap adopted in 1979. Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has grown far faster than inflation or population and that the state budget rises and falls with the fortunes of a small number of high-income taxpayers. Proposition 41 is best read as an attempt to restore discipline to that budget. It also contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would void the billionaire tax on the same ballot (see California Decides, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0040A1).
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Starting retroactively on January 1, 2026, any program that would be the recipient of new or increased special tax revenues as a result of a citizen initiative must undergo state performance audits prior to the vote. Such programs, and those receiving revenues from legislatively enacted new or increased special taxes, must be audited every four years thereafter. No new state tax or increase to a state tax enacted on or after that date may route its revenue outside California’s voter-approved spending limit, commonly referred to as the Gann limit.
A vote NO means: California keeps current law. New special taxes are not subject to this audit regime, and new taxes may continue to direct revenue into funds that sit outside the Gann limit, as several existing taxes already do.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0040A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0040 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-040)
1. Overview
Proposition 41 would add a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. It has two main provisions.
The first provision is an audit requirement for programs that would receive funds from proposed special tax initiatives. A special tax is one whose revenue is dedicated to specific purposes rather than available for general use. When the proponents of a citizen initiative that would create a new or increased special tax notify the secretary of state that they have gathered 25 percent of the required signatures, the state auditor must begin a financial and performance audit of each program the special tax would fund. The audit must assess program effectiveness, evaluate the potential for fraud, waste, and abuse, and recommend ways the program could achieve budgetary savings of at least 10 percent a year. If the measure qualifies for the ballot, an executive summary of the audit must be printed in the state voter information guide.
A subsequent audit must be repeated every four years for every new or increased special tax enacted by the legislature or by voters on or after January 1, 2026. When a tax passes, the audit costs are reimbursed from the tax’s own revenue. When a tax initiative fails to qualify or is rejected, the general fund absorbs the cost.
The second provision protects the state spending limit from being circumvented by future state taxes. The Gann limit, adopted by voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and amended by Proposition 111 in 1990, caps how much tax revenue the state may appropriate each year. It’s adjusted for increases to population and per capita income, and some substantial categories of spending are excluded from the cap. According to the Gann limit, if tax revenue exceeds the limit over two consecutive years the excess revenue must be split between taxpayer rebates and additional K–14 school funding. For context, rapid tax revenue growth has rarely resulted in mandatory Gann limit rebates.
However, under current rules a new tax can be written to deposit its revenue in a fund that is excluded from the appropriations counted against the Gann limit. Proposition 41 would forbid that design for any state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative, but the ban is limited to taxes that take effect on or after January 1, 2026. New special taxes would still be permitted, but their revenue would simply count toward the same spending cap that applies to other nonexempt tax revenues.
The second provision connects Proposition 41 to Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act. If Prop 40 is approved it would route its revenue into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the structure of the Gann limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. Proposition 41 prohibits new or increased state taxes from circumventing the structure intended to limit the growth of California government spending, and it includes specific text that will nullify Proposition 40 if both initiatives pass but Proposition 41 receives more yes votes.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0040A1, “The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf) (eight pages, amended language submitted January 12, 2026).
Key language:
“No state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 shall be exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation. The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 if the state tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.”
What it amends: Adds a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. The article defines “Government Spending Limitation” as Article XIII B, the Gann limit, and defines an exempted tax as one whose revenue is deposited outside the general fund and left out of the appropriations subject to the limit or that raises the appropriations limit by statute.
Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it. The measure also includes a self-defense provision that appoints and funds independent counsel through a continuous general fund appropriation if the governor and attorney general decline to defend it.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
It would create constitutionally required audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, both before a tax initiative reaches voters and every four years after a tax takes effect. It also creates a ban on excluding the revenue from any new or increased state tax from the Gann spending limit.
Where?
Statewide, written into the California Constitution.
When?
It takes effect on passage and reaches back to taxes enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The initiative’s authors frame it as a response to California’s nation-leading tax rates and their effect on the state’s affordability crisis. The stated purpose is to require up-front, recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes and to prevent new taxes from circumventing the Gann limit so that surplus revenue is refunded rather than spent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Audit requirements of Proposition 41 address a documented problem. For example, in 2024 the state auditor found that California spent roughly $24 billion on homelessness and housing programs over five fiscal years without consistently tracking whether the money reduced homelessness. Three of the five programs reviewed did not produce enough data to judge their cost-effectiveness at all. Proposition 41 would make that kind of review routine for programs funded by new special taxes, and it would give voters an audit summary before they vote on a tax initiative. Independent, recurring performance audits with concrete savings targets are the kind of accountability that good-government advocates across the spectrum have long sought.
Proposition 41’s requirement that future special taxes be subject to the Gann limit is similarly reasonable: California’s fiscal challenge is accelerated spending, not a shortage of revenue. Research by Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Lee Ohanian shows that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population fell by almost 500,000 people, while the state budget grew nearly 57 percent (31 percent after inflation). Additional research by Hoover fellows Lanhee J. Chen and Joshua D. Rauh describes how California’s heavy reliance on the personal income tax, which now supplies most general fund tax revenue, ties the budget to the performance of the stock market. In 2021, the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue. Meanwhile, the state budget swung $175 billion from a surplus in 2022 to a deficit in 2024.
The Gann limit is one of the few constitutional tools that restrains government spending growth during economic booms that becomes a fiscal catastrophe during leaner times. Prior analysis by Hoover Fellow Bill Whalen has traced how the Gann limit’s fiscal discipline has been eroded over time, from Proposition 111’s 1990 exclusion of new gas tax revenue to budgeting practices that kept billions out of the limit calculation. Proposition 41 would close the special-fund circumvention for any future tax.
Importantly, Prop 41 does not ban new taxes, nor does it cut existing programs. It simply requires that revenue from any new tax be counted alongside the rest of state spending, so that a future surplus is dedicated to a tax rebate and additional school funding (per Prop 4 and Prop 111) rather than accumulating in a dedicated fund. This rule should help encourage policymakers to be more thoughtful about expanding government programs when tax revenues unexpectedly increase.
Like Proposition 42, Proposition 41 contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferable to asking the courts to decide which parts of two conflicting constitutional amendments survive.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 41 would require any programs receiving funding from new or increased special taxes to be audited by the state auditor to assess performance, evaluate potential for waste, fraud, and abuse, and identify explicit cost savings opportunities. It would also require each new state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative to be subject to the Gann limit. Its most immediate effect would be to nullify Proposition 40 if it draws more yes votes, while its lasting effect would be to hold all future state taxes to the same spending cap as the rest of the budget.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s fiscal problem is driven by spending increases that have managed to outstrip even the state’s strong tax revenue growth. From that perspective, Proposition 41 would offer increased oversight on how well California is spending taxpayer dollars.

This wealth tax is short-sighted, self-sabotaging. However, the countermeasures written by billionaires go too far, restricting future generations from tackling AI-induced economic uncertainties

By Bay Area News Group Editorial Board (https://www.record-bee.com/author/bay-area-news-group-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 27, 2026 at 6:36 AM PDT

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.
Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40. And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

## What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot.
(Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.)
All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.

Regarding Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) , California could use better audits of spending programs. It’s a good idea to identify ways to trim existing programs before shoveling more money their way. It is taxpayers’ money, after all. Requiring audits after election officials have collected only 25% of qualifying signatures imposes a relatively costly burden, but those expenses are a rounding error for any major program. We also believe the state should better live up to the terms of the Gann Limit.
Regarding Prop. 42 (https://yesonprop42.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=YesOn42&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24250385746&gbraid=0AAAABEi2smx27CdnofkbhPlt_FqIHXDrD&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHUyIfjJPNFkY5WqUynwZ9APOIPtTZDTa7v5_wEBmvD8nV21v3IkUbhoCCZ8QAvD_BwE) , we endorse its efforts to limit unreasonable future tax increases. G oing back and raising taxes on past earnings (as Prop. 40 does) before the new law was passed is unseemly. Opponents complain that it ties the hands of future Legislatures, but we’re totally fine with putting certain types of assets outside the revenuers’ grasp.
Vote yes on Propositions 41 and 42.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed initiative regarding special taxes (A.G. File No. 25-0040, Amendment #1).
Background
Special Tax. Taxes are a type of revenue that can be used to support any public purpose. Some state taxes are unrestricted, meaning that revenues raised by these taxes can be used to fund any program. In contrast, a special tax is a tax levied on a specific good (for example, tobacco or fuel) or activity (for example, waste disposal or energy use) to raise revenue for a specific state program. Taxes can be raised by the Legislature, by a two-thirds vote, or by voters with a majority vote.
California State Auditor's Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government that evaluates state and local governments' financial and operational activities. The State Auditor's work includes financial and policy evaluations (also known as performance audits) where the auditor assesses the extent to which a governmental entity efficiently and effectively carries out requirements in law. As part of its audit, the State Auditor may present recommendations for the entity to improve its operations. Some of the State Auditor's audits are recurring to ensure ongoing compliance with the law while others are
one time in nature.
Proposal
One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on Ballot Through Initiative Process. The measure would require the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of proposed citizen initiatives that contain a special tax once proponents notify the Secretary of State that 25 percent of the necessary voter signatures to qualify the initiative for the ballot have been collected. The measure would require these audits to (1) evaluate each program that would receive funding from the special tax contained in the proposed initiative and (2) address specific issues identified by the measure including assessing the efficiency of the program and recommending how the audited program could reduce its annual costs by 10 percent. The measure also would require the State Auditor to produce an executive summary of the audit. If the initiative qualifies for the ballot, the measure would require this executive summary to be included in the Voter Information Guide (VIG) produced by the Secretary of State . If approved by the voters, the measure would require the State Auditor to be reimbursed from the revenues generated by the special tax.
Recurring Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From Future Special Taxes. The measure would require the State Auditor to conduct recurring financial and performance audits every four years of programs funded by special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. In addition to the issues that would be required of the one-time audits previously described, the measure would require the audits to include the State Auditor's recommendations to improve program efficiency. The State Auditor would be required to solicit public input while preparing the audits. Under the measure, the State Auditor's costs to conduct a recurring audit would be reimbursed from the revenues generated by the special tax.
Fiscal Effects
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. When a ballot measure contains a special tax, the measure would require the VIG to include the State Auditor's executive summary. This could add several pages to the VIG and increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Reimbursement Costs to State Auditor When Proposed Initiatives Fail. If an initiative containing a special tax were approved by voters, the revenues from the special tax would be used to reimburse the State Auditor for costs incurred related to the one-time and ongoing audits required under the measure. If such an initiative were rejected by voters or received 25 percent of required signatures but ultimately did not qualify for the ballot, the state General Fund would pay the cost of the one-time audit, likely varying case to case but totaling in the range of the low millions of dollars for each two-year election cycle.
Possible Effects if Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. To the extent that programs were to adopt the State Auditor's recommendations in an audit, the measure could result in savings or improved services at existing funding levels. The degree to which this would occur depends on future decisions and are not known.
Summary of Fiscal Impacts. We estimate that the measure would have the following fiscal effects:
Unknown Fiscal Effect. Net costs or savings resulting from the measure would depend on (1) how many special tax initiatives qualify for a one-time audit but are not approved by voters, (2) the number of pages that are added to the Voter Information Guide each election cycle, and (3) the level of savings that are identified and implemented as a result of the audits.

Overview of the Spending Plan
Introduction
Budget Choices
General Fund Condition
Evolution of the Budget
Major Features
Introduction
Each year, our office publishes the California Spending Plan to summarize the annual state budget. In this publication we provide an overview of the 2026‑27 budget package, give a brief description of how the budget process unfolded, and then highlight the major features of the budget approved by the Legislature and signed by the Governor. This publication reflects the administration's estimates of legislative actions taken through the end of June 2026. In addition to this report, we will release a series of issue‑specific, online posts that give more detail on the major actions in the budget package.
Budget Choices
In most years, we would describe the size of the budget problem (or budget surplus) the Legislature addressed (or allocated) and the mix of choices that make up that total. This year, neither framing fits the budget package as neatly. Although the budget package includes some traditional budget solutions, it also reflects a substantial amount of new discretionary spending and a large, first‑time deposit into a surplus holding account. Taken together, these choices roughly offset one another. At the same time, the budget continues to rely on reserve capacity, even as revenues have surged to levels only surpassed by the state's previous peak in 2021‑22. Taken altogether, this makes the budget condition difficult to describe concisely. As such, this section describes the state's budget choices on both sides of the ledger: first new commitments and discretionary choices, and then the budget solutions made.
New Commitments
Revenue and Spending Commitments
New Discretionary Spending Totals Nearly $6 Billion. The budget commits $5.7 billion in new, discretionary General Fund money in 2026‑27. We define discretionary spending as new spending or revenue reductions that were not previously authorized under current law or legislative policy. Nearly all of these commitments are spending related-revenue reductions account for only about $25 million of the total, mainly a temporary reduction in the minimum franchise tax for newly formed businesses. For context, this new discretionary spending is equivalent to roughly 90 percent of the total year‑over‑year growth in General Fund spending between 2025‑26 and 2026‑27. A list of the discretionary General Fund spending actions (excluding Proposition 98 (1988)) in the 2026‑27 budget package are listed in Appendix 1.
Most New Spending Is One Time, but the Budget Also Added New Ongoing Costs. Of the $5.7 billion in new discretionary spending, about $5 billion (87 percent) is one time, while the remaining roughly $700 million reflects ongoing commitments-costs that will recur as part of the budget's baseline in future years. On a fully phased‑in basis, these will total about $825 million annually. This new ongoing spending is a relatively small share of the total. Nonetheless, it adds to the budget's baseline costs in future years, offsetting the solutions described elsewhere in this report that were used to address the gap between the state's ongoing revenues and expenditures.
New Spending Is Concentrated in Health, Though New Spending Touches Nearly Every Program Area. With over 250 individual items, new discretionary spending reaches nearly every part of the budget, but on a programmatic basis, health programs account for the largest share (nearly 40 percent of the total), followed by general government, labor, and related programs (15 percent); housing and homelessness (12 percent); and criminal justice (11 percent). Human services and resources and environment programs each account for about 8 percent to 9 percent, with the remainder split between higher education (3 percent), K‑14 education (excluding Proposition 98) (2 percent), and transportation (1 percent). Within health, the largest commitments are two one‑time actions that delay previously planned reductions to Medi‑Cal safety net clinic and dental payments ($1 billion and $258 million, respectively), along with $361 million for dental benefits for adults with unsatisfactory immigration status (UIS) and $250 million in public hospital grants. Other large individual commitments outside of health include: (1) $400 million for the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention program (HHAP); (2) $228 million for new child care slots, plus $112 million to increase the child care monthly cost of care; (3) $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program; and (4) $150 million each for the Community Air Protection Program and judicial branch deferred maintenance. Beyond these larger items, the remainder of the new augmentations consist of many smaller commitments-the median item is about $5 million-reflecting a broad range of initiatives.
Discretionary Reserves and Set Asides
Sets Discretionary Reserve Balance to $4.5 Billion. The Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties (SFEU) is a general‑purpose reserve commonly used to provide capacity for unanticipated expenditures, including state costs associated with disasters and other emergencies. On a technical basis, it can be thought of as the end balance of the state's General Fund-the money that remains after accounting for all of the state's expected revenues and spending. The State Constitution has a balanced budget requirement, which means the balance of the SFEU must be set at zero or above for the upcoming fiscal year (2026‑27). Any level above that is up to the discretion of the Legislature. As a result, we consider the entire balance of the SFEU to be a discretionary choice. The budget sets the SFEU balance at $4.5 billion, in line with recent budgets, which have set the balance between $3.5 billion and $4.5 billion.
Makes $6.4 Billion Transfer to Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA). The budget package deposits $6.4 billion into the TSHA, to be withdrawn in 2027‑28. Importantly, neither our office nor the Department of Finance considers this account to be a reserve. That is because, while it can help the state manage surging revenues within the budget window, it cannot mitigate against a future downturn in revenues. The box below describes this account and the transfer in more detail.
What Is the Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA)?
Revenues Are Both Volatile and Uncertain. State revenues are volatile-they can grow or shrink rapidly from year to year, particularly because California's tax system relies heavily on high‑income taxpayers. This means that, in some years, the state will collect significantly less in tax revenue than needed to cover its spending commitments-resulting in large budget problems. Relatedly, there is significant uncertainty about near‑term revenue estimates-that is, even for the upcoming fiscal year, revenues can come in significantly above or below projections, resulting in large forecasting errors. This is especially common when revenues are growing or shrinking rapidly.
TSHA Was Set Up to Avoid Overspending a Surplus. In 2024, the Legislature created the TSHA as a tool intended to manage near‑term revenue uncertainty. The account was designed for periods when the state has a surplus driven by rapid revenue growth and might otherwise commit to new spending based on revenue estimates that later prove overstated. The Legislature initially considered establishing formulas or rules governing deposits into the account. Ultimately, however, the TSHA was enacted as a flexible and largely discretionary mechanism.
Budget Uses TSHA for the First Time. The 2026‑27 budget package deposits $6.4 billion into the TSHA and plans to withdraw the same amount in 2027‑28. (By law, funds can remain in the account for up to one year.) In effect, this transfer uses anticipated 2026‑27 resources to help balance the following year's budget, rather than allocating those resources to new purposes in the current budget window.
Budget Solutions
The state has several types of solutions-or options-for addressing a shortfall between resources and costs, but the most important include: reserve withdrawals, spending reductions, revenue increases, and borrowing (for example, loaning money from other funds to the General Fund).
Budget Package Included $14 Billion in Budget Solutions. The budget package includes about $14 billion in budget solutions. This total is essentially the same as the amount in the Governor's May Revision (also $14 billion). Figure 1 summarizes the solutions that the budget package used. As the figure shows, the budget primarily relies on reserves and borrowing, which together represent about two‑thirds of total solutions. Spending‑related solutions-reductions and fund shifts-represent about $3 billion, or roughly one‑fifth of the total. Revenue‑related solutions, at $2 billion, represent the remainder. This section provides additional detail on each category of solution. Appendix 2 lists all the budget solutions.
Reserves ($5 Billion)
Nearly 40 percent of the budget's solutions are achieved by suspending an otherwise required reserve deposit-$5.4 billion. This is the single largest category of solutions in the budget package.
Suspends Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) True‑Up Deposit of $5.4 Billion. Proposition 2 (2014) outlines the formulas by which the state must, each year, make deposits into the BSA, unless those requirements are suspended under a budget emergency. Proposition 2 also requires the state to revisit-or "true up"-its estimates of BSA deposits twice: once in each subsequent fiscal year. These true ups are required even if the initial deposit was suspended; however, true ups can themselves be suspended, as well. The state already suspended a $1.6 billion initial deposit for 2025‑26. Under the administration's revenue estimates, an additional $5.4 billion true‑up deposit was otherwise required for that year. The budget package suspends this entire true‑up deposit.
Borrowing ($4 Billion)
The budget package addresses about one‑quarter of its solutions using borrowing-$3.9 billion. We define "borrowing" as budget actions that achieve savings in the present but result in an obligation or higher cost for the state in a future year.
Entire Borrowing Total Reflects a Proposition 98 " Settle‑Up" Obligation. This year's borrowing consists of a single action: a $3.9 billion Proposition 98 settle‑up obligation. Proposition 98 sets a minimum funding requirement for schools and community colleges based on formulas in the State Constitution. The state makes an initial estimate of this requirement when it enacts the budget, then revises this estimate over the following two years to reflect updated data. The budget funds schools and community colleges below the current estimate of the minimum requirement for 2025‑26, which provides temporary budget capacity but requires the state to settle up using future revenues. (This is why we categorize settle up as borrowing: it produces savings today at the cost of an obligation the state will need to pay later.)
The Administration Does Not Currently Publish a List of Outstanding Budgetary Borrowing. The borrowing described in this section is similar to the array of measures used during the Great Recession-collectively referred to at the time as the state's "wall of debt"-which created obligations to address budget gaps and that the state repaid or reversed gradually over time. While the state has various financial and accounting reports that allow policymakers and observers to track certain kinds of liabilities, the administration does not produce an easily accessible, public list that consolidates the state's outstanding budgetary borrowing incurred to address recent budget problems. We provide our best estimate of this list in Figure 2 .

We Estimate the State's Outstanding Budgetary Borrowing Will Total $29 Billion at the End of 2026‑27. As figure 2 shows, under the budget package, we estimate the state will have about $29 billion in outstanding budgetary borrowing at the end of 2026‑27. This total includes the $3.9 billion Proposition 98 settle‑up obligation described earlier in this section. The value of existing obligations can also change from year to year based on repayments and new borrowing, but also updated estimates and other budget actions. For example, the amount of borrowing for the Middle Class Scholarship program has declined, reflecting a budgetary decision to lower award coverage (from 35 percent to 23 percent of students' remaining financial need). The budget package also includes an extension of the business credit limitation, which was set to expire in 2026, and now will expire in 2029.
Spending‑Related Solutions ($3 Billion)
Fund Shifts. We estimate the budget package includes about $2.4 billion in fund shifts, nearly all of which are concentrated in Medi‑Cal and other health programs. The largest is a $1.7 billion shift that uses Proposition 35 (2024) managed care organization (MCO) tax funds to cover provider payment increases that otherwise would have been supported by the General Fund. Other notable fund shifts include $387 million in MCO tax funds redirected to support behavioral health spending and a combined $212 million in Behavioral Health Services Fund offsets across the Department of Health Care Services, the Department of Public Health, and the Department of Health Care Access and Information.
Reductions ($0.6 Billion). We estimate the budget package includes about $580 million in spending reductions. These are concentrated in child care and Medi‑Cal. The largest include a $212 million reduction to State Preschool to align funding with program costs, a $127 million reduction to child care slots, and a $48 million reduction to the child care cost‑of‑living adjustment (COLA). In addition, the budget package extends new work requirements and six‑month renewal periods to Medi‑Cal enrollees with UIS, which results in $60 million in savings in 2026‑27, growing to roughly $1.2 billion in savings in 2027‑28, and $2 billion in savings ongoing.
Revenue‑Related Solutions ($2 Billion)
Includes $2 Billion in Revenue‑Related Solutions. The budget package includes three ongoing revenue solutions. The largest extends a temporary cap on business tax credits for three additional years before making the limitation permanent beginning in 2030, providing $1 billion in 2026‑27. The budget also renews the MCO tax, providing $575 million in General Fund savings in 2026‑27, and extends the sales tax to certain digital software sales, raising $450 million in 2026‑27. Each of these is described in more detail in the "Major Features" section below.
General Fund Condition
In this section, we describe the overall condition of the General Fund budget and provide state appropriations limit (SAL) estimates under the spending plan. As is the case in the previous section, the figures here use the administration's budget estimates as of June 2026.
Budget Window
Figure 3 summarizes the condition of the General Fund under the revenue and spending assumptions in the June 2026 budget package, as estimated by the administration. Under these projections, the state ends 2026‑27 with $4.5 billion in the SFEU. (The SFEU is the state's operating reserve and essentially functions like an end‑of‑year balance.) The revised balance of $29.2 billion in the SFEU for 2025‑26 reflects, in large part, a significant upward revision to 2025‑26 revenues. That revenue upgrade leaves the budget close to structurally balanced in that year but does not carry through to 2026‑27, as the administration assumes revenues are essentially flat in 2026‑27. As a result, drawing down that elevated 2025‑26 balance-along with other choices described earlier in this report-allows the state to cover costs in 2026‑27 that would not otherwise be covered by that year's revenues on their own. In other words, the state has a structural imbalance in 2026‑27, even though the enacted budget is balanced.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Summary
Support
Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Oppose
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Support
Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

A.G. File No. 2025-040
January 27, 2026
PDF Version (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250544.PDF)
Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed initiative regarding special taxes (A.G. File No. 25-0040, Amendment #1).
Background
Special Tax. Taxes are a type of revenue that can be used to support any public purpose. Some state taxes are unrestricted, meaning that revenues raised by these taxes can be used to fund any program. In contrast, a special tax is a tax levied on a specific good (for example, tobacco or fuel) or activity (for example, waste disposal or energy use) to raise revenue for a specific state program. Taxes can be raised by the Legislature, by a two-thirds vote, or by voters with a majority vote.
California State Auditor's Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government that evaluates state and local governments' financial and operational activities. The State Auditor's work includes financial and policy evaluations (also known as performance audits) where the auditor assesses the extent to which a governmental entity efficiently and effectively carries out requirements in law. As part of its audit, the State Auditor may present recommendations for the entity to improve its operations. Some of the State Auditor's audits are recurring to ensure ongoing compliance with the law while others are
one time in nature.
Proposal
One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on Ballot Through Initiative Process. The measure would require the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of proposed citizen initiatives that contain a special tax once proponents notify the Secretary of State that 25 percent of the necessary voter signatures to qualify the initiative for the ballot have been collected. The measure would require these audits to (1) evaluate each program that would receive funding from the special tax contained in the proposed initiative and (2) address specific issues identified by the measure including assessing the efficiency of the program and recommending how the audited program could reduce its annual costs by 10 percent. The measure also would require the State Auditor to produce an executive summary of the audit. If the initiative qualifies for the ballot, the measure would require this executive summary to be included in the Voter Information Guide (VIG) produced by the Secretary of State . If approved by the voters, the measure would require the State Auditor to be reimbursed from the revenues generated by the special tax.
Recurring Audits of Programs Receiving Funds From Future Special Taxes. The measure would require the State Auditor to conduct recurring financial and performance audits every four years of programs funded by special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026. In addition to the issues that would be required of the one-time audits previously described, the measure would require the audits to include the State Auditor's recommendations to improve program efficiency. The State Auditor would be required to solicit public input while preparing the audits. Under the measure, the State Auditor's costs to conduct a recurring audit would be reimbursed from the revenues generated by the special tax.
Fiscal Effects
Higher Costs to Print and Mail VIG. When a ballot measure contains a special tax, the measure would require the VIG to include the State Auditor's executive summary. This could add several pages to the VIG and increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.
Reimbursement Costs to State Auditor When Proposed Initiatives Fail. If an initiative containing a special tax were approved by voters, the revenues from the special tax would be used to reimburse the State Auditor for costs incurred related to the one-time and ongoing audits required under the measure. If such an initiative were rejected by voters or received 25 percent of required signatures but ultimately did not qualify for the ballot, the state General Fund would pay the cost of the one-time audit, likely varying case to case but totaling in the range of the low millions of dollars for each two-year election cycle.
Possible Effects if Auditor Recommendations Are Implemented. To the extent that programs were to adopt the State Auditor's recommendations in an audit, the measure could result in savings or improved services at existing funding levels. The degree to which this would occur depends on future decisions and are not known.
Summary of Fiscal Impacts. We estimate that the measure would have the following fiscal effects:
Unknown Fiscal Effect. Net costs or savings resulting from the measure would depend on (1) how many special tax initiatives qualify for a one-time audit but are not approved by voters, (2) the number of pages that are added to the Voter Information Guide each election cycle, and (3) the level of savings that are identified and implemented as a result of the audits.

Introduction
Each year, our office publishes the California Spending Plan to summarize the annual state budget. In this publication we provide an overview of the 2026‑27 budget package, give a brief description of how the budget process unfolded, and then highlight the major features of the budget approved by the Legislature and signed by the Governor. This publication reflects the administration's estimates of legislative actions taken through the end of June 2026. In addition to this report, we will release a series of issue‑specific, online posts that give more detail on the major actions in the budget package.
Budget Choices
In most years, we would describe the size of the budget problem (or budget surplus) the Legislature addressed (or allocated) and the mix of choices that make up that total. This year, neither framing fits the budget package as neatly. Although the budget package includes some traditional budget solutions, it also reflects a substantial amount of new discretionary spending and a large, first‑time deposit into a surplus holding account. Taken together, these choices roughly offset one another. At the same time, the budget continues to rely on reserve capacity, even as revenues have surged to levels only surpassed by the state's previous peak in 2021‑22. Taken altogether, this makes the budget condition difficult to describe concisely. As such, this section describes the state's budget choices on both sides of the ledger: first new commitments and discretionary choices, and then the budget solutions made.
New Commitments
Revenue and Spending Commitments
New Discretionary Spending Totals Nearly $6 Billion. The budget commits $5.7 billion in new, discretionary General Fund money in 2026‑27. We define discretionary spending as new spending or revenue reductions that were not previously authorized under current law or legislative policy. Nearly all of these commitments are spending related-revenue reductions account for only about $25 million of the total, mainly a temporary reduction in the minimum franchise tax for newly formed businesses. For context, this new discretionary spending is equivalent to roughly 90 percent of the total year‑over‑year growth in General Fund spending between 2025‑26 and 2026‑27. A list of the discretionary General Fund spending actions (excluding Proposition 98 (1988)) in the 2026‑27 budget package are listed in Appendix 1.
Most New Spending Is One Time, but the Budget Also Added New Ongoing Costs. Of the $5.7 billion in new discretionary spending, about $5 billion (87 percent) is one time, while the remaining roughly $700 million reflects ongoing commitments-costs that will recur as part of the budget's baseline in future years. On a fully phased‑in basis, these will total about $825 million annually. This new ongoing spending is a relatively small share of the total. Nonetheless, it adds to the budget's baseline costs in future years, offsetting the solutions described elsewhere in this report that were used to address the gap between the state's ongoing revenues and expenditures.
New Spending Is Concentrated in Health, Though New Spending Touches Nearly Every Program Area. With over 250 individual items, new discretionary spending reaches nearly every part of the budget, but on a programmatic basis, health programs account for the largest share (nearly 40 percent of the total), followed by general government, labor, and related programs (15 percent); housing and homelessness (12 percent); and criminal justice (11 percent). Human services and resources and environment programs each account for about 8 percent to 9 percent, with the remainder split between higher education (3 percent), K‑14 education (excluding Proposition 98) (2 percent), and transportation (1 percent). Within health, the largest commitments are two one‑time actions that delay previously planned reductions to Medi‑Cal safety net clinic and dental payments ($1 billion and $258 million, respectively), along with $361 million for dental benefits for adults with unsatisfactory immigration status (UIS) and $250 million in public hospital grants. Other large individual commitments outside of health include: (1) $400 million for the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention program (HHAP); (2) $228 million for new child care slots, plus $112 million to increase the child care monthly cost of care; (3) $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program; and (4) $150 million each for the Community Air Protection Program and judicial branch deferred maintenance. Beyond these larger items, the remainder of the new augmentations consist of many smaller commitments-the median item is about $5 million-reflecting a broad range of initiatives.
Discretionary Reserves and Set Asides
Sets Discretionary Reserve Balance to $4.5 Billion. The Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties (SFEU) is a general‑purpose reserve commonly used to provide capacity for unanticipated expenditures, including state costs associated with disasters and other emergencies. On a technical basis, it can be thought of as the end balance of the state's General Fund-the money that remains after accounting for all of the state's expected revenues and spending. The State Constitution has a balanced budget requirement, which means the balance of the SFEU must be set at zero or above for the upcoming fiscal year (2026‑27). Any level above that is up to the discretion of the Legislature. As a result, we consider the entire balance of the SFEU to be a discretionary choice. The budget sets the SFEU balance at $4.5 billion, in line with recent budgets, which have set the balance between $3.5 billion and $4.5 billion.
Makes $6.4 Billion Transfer to Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA). The budget package deposits $6.4 billion into the TSHA, to be withdrawn in 2027‑28. Importantly, neither our office nor the Department of Finance considers this account to be a reserve. That is because, while it can help the state manage surging revenues within the budget window, it cannot mitigate against a future downturn in revenues. The box below describes this account and the transfer in more detail.
What Is the Temporary Surplus Holding Account (TSHA)?
Revenues Are Both Volatile and Uncertain. State revenues are volatile-they can grow or shrink rapidly from year to year, particularly because California's tax system relies heavily on high‑income taxpayers. This means that, in some years, the state will collect significantly less in tax revenue than needed to cover its spending commitments-resulting in large budget problems. Relatedly, there is significant uncertainty about near‑term revenue estimates-that is, even for the upcoming fiscal year, revenues can come in significantly above or below projections, resulting in large forecasting errors. This is especially common when revenues are growing or shrinking rapidly.
TSHA Was Set Up to Avoid Overspending a Surplus. In 2024, the Legislature created the TSHA as a tool intended to manage near‑term revenue uncertainty. The account was designed for periods when the state has a surplus driven by rapid revenue growth and might otherwise commit to new spending based on revenue estimates that later prove overstated. The Legislature initially considered establishing formulas or rules governing deposits into the account. Ultimately, however, the TSHA was enacted as a flexible and largely discretionary mechanism.
Budget Uses TSHA for the First Time. The 2026‑27 budget package deposits $6.4 billion into the TSHA and plans to withdraw the same amount in 2027‑28. (By law, funds can remain in the account for up to one year.) In effect, this transfer uses anticipated 2026‑27 resources to help balance the following year's budget, rather than allocating those resources to new purposes in the current budget window.
Budget Solutions
The state has several types of solutions-or options-for addressing a shortfall between resources and costs, but the most important include: reserve withdrawals, spending reductions, revenue increases, and borrowing (for example, loaning money from other funds to the General Fund).
Budget Package Included $14 Billion in Budget Solutions. The budget package includes about $14 billion in budget solutions. This total is essentially the same as the amount in the Governor's May Revision (also $14 billion). Figure 1 summarizes the solutions that the budget package used. As the figure shows, the budget primarily relies on reserves and borrowing, which together represent about two‑thirds of total solutions. Spending‑related solutions-reductions and fund shifts-represent about $3 billion, or roughly one‑fifth of the total. Revenue‑related solutions, at $2 billion, represent the remainder. This section provides additional detail on each category of solution. Appendix 2 lists all the budget solutions.
Reserves ($5 Billion)
Nearly 40 percent of the budget's solutions are achieved by suspending an otherwise required reserve deposit-$5.4 billion. This is the single largest category of solutions in the budget package.
Suspends Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) True‑Up Deposit of $5.4 Billion. Proposition 2 (2014) outlines the formulas by which the state must, each year, make deposits into the BSA, unless those requirements are suspended under a budget emergency. Proposition 2 also requires the state to revisit-or "true up"-its estimates of BSA deposits twice: once in each subsequent fiscal year. These true ups are required even if the initial deposit was suspended; however, true ups can themselves be suspended, as well. The state already suspended a $1.6 billion initial deposit for 2025‑26. Under the administration's revenue estimates, an additional $5.4 billion true‑up deposit was otherwise required for that year. The budget package suspends this entire true‑up deposit.
Borrowing ($4 Billion)
The budget package addresses about one‑quarter of its solutions using borrowing-$3.9 billion. We define "borrowing" as budget actions that achieve savings in the present but result in an obligation or higher cost for the state in a future year.
Entire Borrowing Total Reflects a Proposition 98 " Settle‑Up" Obligation. This year's borrowing consists of a single action: a $3.9 billion Proposition 98 settle‑up obligation. Proposition 98 sets a minimum funding requirement for schools and community colleges based on formulas in the State Constitution. The state makes an initial estimate of this requirement when it enacts the budget, then revises this estimate over the following two years to reflect updated data. The budget funds schools and community colleges below the current estimate of the minimum requirement for 2025‑26, which provides temporary budget capacity but requires the state to settle up using future revenues. (This is why we categorize settle up as borrowing: it produces savings today at the cost of an obligation the state will need to pay later.)
The Administration Does Not Currently Publish a List of Outstanding Budgetary Borrowing. The borrowing described in this section is similar to the array of measures used during the Great Recession-collectively referred to at the time as the state's "wall of debt"-which created obligations to address budget gaps and that the state repaid or reversed gradually over time. While the state has various financial and accounting reports that allow policymakers and observers to track certain kinds of liabilities, the administration does not produce an easily accessible, public list that consolidates the state's outstanding budgetary borrowing incurred to address recent budget problems. We provide our best estimate of this list in Figure 2 .

We Estimate the State's Outstanding Budgetary Borrowing Will Total $29 Billion at the End of 2026‑27. As figure 2 shows, under the budget package, we estimate the state will have about $29 billion in outstanding budgetary borrowing at the end of 2026‑27. This total includes the $3.9 billion Proposition 98 settle‑up obligation described earlier in this section. The value of existing obligations can also change from year to year based on repayments and new borrowing, but also updated estimates and other budget actions. For example, the amount of borrowing for the Middle Class Scholarship program has declined, reflecting a budgetary decision to lower award coverage (from 35 percent to 23 percent of students' remaining financial need). The budget package also includes an extension of the business credit limitation, which was set to expire in 2026, and now will expire in 2029.
Spending‑Related Solutions ($3 Billion)
Fund Shifts. We estimate the budget package includes about $2.4 billion in fund shifts, nearly all of which are concentrated in Medi‑Cal and other health programs. The largest is a $1.7 billion shift that uses Proposition 35 (2024) managed care organization (MCO) tax funds to cover provider payment increases that otherwise would have been supported by the General Fund. Other notable fund shifts include $387 million in MCO tax funds redirected to support behavioral health spending and a combined $212 million in Behavioral Health Services Fund offsets across the Department of Health Care Services, the Department of Public Health, and the Department of Health Care Access and Information.
Reductions ($0.6 Billion). We estimate the budget package includes about $580 million in spending reductions. These are concentrated in child care and Medi‑Cal. The largest include a $212 million reduction to State Preschool to align funding with program costs, a $127 million reduction to child care slots, and a $48 million reduction to the child care cost‑of‑living adjustment (COLA). In addition, the budget package extends new work requirements and six‑month renewal periods to Medi‑Cal enrollees with UIS, which results in $60 million in savings in 2026‑27, growing to roughly $1.2 billion in savings in 2027‑28, and $2 billion in savings ongoing.
Revenue‑Related Solutions ($2 Billion)
Includes $2 Billion in Revenue‑Related Solutions. The budget package includes three ongoing revenue solutions. The largest extends a temporary cap on business tax credits for three additional years before making the limitation permanent beginning in 2030, providing $1 billion in 2026‑27. The budget also renews the MCO tax, providing $575 million in General Fund savings in 2026‑27, and extends the sales tax to certain digital software sales, raising $450 million in 2026‑27. Each of these is described in more detail in the "Major Features" section below.
General Fund Condition
In this section, we describe the overall condition of the General Fund budget and provide state appropriations limit (SAL) estimates under the spending plan. As is the case in the previous section, the figures here use the administration's budget estimates as of June 2026.
Budget Window
Figure 3 summarizes the condition of the General Fund under the revenue and spending assumptions in the June 2026 budget package, as estimated by the administration. Under these projections, the state ends 2026‑27 with $4.5 billion in the SFEU. (The SFEU is the state's operating reserve and essentially functions like an end‑of‑year balance.) The revised balance of $29.2 billion in the SFEU for 2025‑26 reflects, in large part, a significant upward revision to 2025‑26 revenues. That revenue upgrade leaves the budget close to structurally balanced in that year but does not carry through to 2026‑27, as the administration assumes revenues are essentially flat in 2026‑27. As a result, drawing down that elevated 2025‑26 balance-along with other choices described earlier in this report-allows the state to cover costs in 2026‑27 that would not otherwise be covered by that year's revenues on their own. In other words, the state has a structural imbalance in 2026‑27, even though the enacted budget is balanced.

We Estimate the State's Outstanding Budgetary Borrowing Will Total $29 Billion at the End of 2026‑27. As figure 2 shows, under the budget package, we estimate the state will have about $29 billion in outstanding budgetary borrowing at the end of 2026‑27. This total includes the $3.9 billion Proposition 98 settle‑up obligation described earlier in this section. The value of existing obligations can also change from year to year based on repayments and new borrowing, but also updated estimates and other budget actions. For example, the amount of borrowing for the Middle Class Scholarship program has declined, reflecting a budgetary decision to lower award coverage (from 35 percent to 23 percent of students' remaining financial need). The budget package also includes an extension of the business credit limitation, which was set to expire in 2026, and now will expire in 2029.
Spending‑Related Solutions ($3 Billion)
Fund Shifts. We estimate the budget package includes about $2.4 billion in fund shifts, nearly all of which are concentrated in Medi‑Cal and other health programs. The largest is a $1.7 billion shift that uses Proposition 35 (2024) managed care organization (MCO) tax funds to cover provider payment increases that otherwise would have been supported by the General Fund. Other notable fund shifts include $387 million in MCO tax funds redirected to support behavioral health spending and a combined $212 million in Behavioral Health Services Fund offsets across the Department of Health Care Services, the Department of Public Health, and the Department of Health Care Access and Information.
Reductions ($0.6 Billion). We estimate the budget package includes about $580 million in spending reductions. These are concentrated in child care and Medi‑Cal. The largest include a $212 million reduction to State Preschool to align funding with program costs, a $127 million reduction to child care slots, and a $48 million reduction to the child care cost‑of‑living adjustment (COLA). In addition, the budget package extends new work requirements and six‑month renewal periods to Medi‑Cal enrollees with UIS, which results in $60 million in savings in 2026‑27, growing to roughly $1.2 billion in savings in 2027‑28, and $2 billion in savings ongoing.
Revenue‑Related Solutions ($2 Billion)
Includes $2 Billion in Revenue‑Related Solutions. The budget package includes three ongoing revenue solutions. The largest extends a temporary cap on business tax credits for three additional years before making the limitation permanent beginning in 2030, providing $1 billion in 2026‑27. The budget also renews the MCO tax, providing $575 million in General Fund savings in 2026‑27, and extends the sales tax to certain digital software sales, raising $450 million in 2026‑27. Each of these is described in more detail in the "Major Features" section below.
General Fund Condition
In this section, we describe the overall condition of the General Fund budget and provide state appropriations limit (SAL) estimates under the spending plan. As is the case in the previous section, the figures here use the administration's budget estimates as of June 2026.
Budget Window
Figure 3 summarizes the condition of the General Fund under the revenue and spending assumptions in the June 2026 budget package, as estimated by the administration. Under these projections, the state ends 2026‑27 with $4.5 billion in the SFEU. (The SFEU is the state's operating reserve and essentially functions like an end‑of‑year balance.) The revised balance of $29.2 billion in the SFEU for 2025‑26 reflects, in large part, a significant upward revision to 2025‑26 revenues. That revenue upgrade leaves the budget close to structurally balanced in that year but does not carry through to 2026‑27, as the administration assumes revenues are essentially flat in 2026‑27. As a result, drawing down that elevated 2025‑26 balance-along with other choices described earlier in this report-allows the state to cover costs in 2026‑27 that would not otherwise be covered by that year's revenues on their own. In other words, the state has a structural imbalance in 2026‑27, even though the enacted budget is balanced.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.
